answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: CLI group: az cosmosdb (core CLI). Example to create a Mongo API account: az cosmosdb create --name MyAccount --resource-group MyRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmo 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." kind = "MongoDB" ... }).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB URI scheme. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@ . TLS (ssl=true) is required; use the SCRAM username/password in the URI or pass credentials to the MongoDB driver. (Port: 10255 for MongoDB over TLS on Cosmos accounts.)

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) uses Request Units (RU/s) as the primary throughput billing model. You can provision throughput at container or database level (manual or autoscale). Cosmos also offers a serverless consumption mode for sporadic workloads. It is not billed by vCores for the MongoDB API (RUs or serverless are the expected billing units).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you normally authenticate with SCRAM username/password credentials defined on the Cosmos account (the MongoDB user). Account keys (primary/master key) are also available for management operations. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not supported for the MongoDB wire protocol in Cosmos DB historically — drivers should use the SCRAM credentials. (Azure AD is supported for some Cosmos DB management/SQL APIs but not as a direct MongoDB driver auth method.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g. pymongo for Python) against the MongoDB-compatible endpoint. There is also the azure-cosmos SDK for the SQL/Core API, but for MongoDB workloads use the MongoDB driver rather than a service-specific 'DocumentDB' SDK.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: As far as I know, Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API does not offer built-in vector index types (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN). Therefore there is no service-side MongoDB command to create vector indexes like createIndex({embedding:'vector'}) WITH engine=... — vector indexes are not supported natively; you must implement vector search via an external service (Cognitive Search custom skill, Azure ML, or a separate vector engine).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB does not provide built-in rich full-text search for the MongoDB API. Typical approach: feed Cosmos DB data into Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) using the change feed or an ETL job and run full-text or hybrid (text + filters) search from Azure Cognitive Search. Alternatively, use external search engines (Elastic, OpenSearch) for text/vector search integration.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB exposes a MongoDB wire protocol compatibility layer — historically support has been for specific MongoDB server versions (e.g. 3.6, 4.0, 4.2 in various regions). Expect some MongoDB server features to be missing or limited: server-side JavaScript (eval), some aggregation stages and operators, certain index types and admin commands, and multi-document transactions or change streams historically have limited or no support on older compatibility versions. Confirm the exact supported MongoDB API version for your account before relying on advanced features.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no MongoDB-compatible local emulator for Cosmos DB's Mongo API. For local development use a local MongoDB instance (official docker image, e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:5.0) and connect on port 27017. The official Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists but historically supports only SQL/Core and some other APIs, not the MongoDB API.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: MongoDB change streams are typically not supported on Cosmos DB's MongoDB API historically. Cosmos DB provides its own change feed feature for the Core/SQL API which can be used to stream updates. For MongoDB-compatible change notifications, you must either use Cosmos DB change feed (if you store data in SQL API) or implement a polling/ETL approach; no MongoDB changeStreams enablement is available historically.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: I would expect the general Azure MCP server (the azure/azure-mcp agent) to include data-plane tooling for Cosmos DB (DocumentDB). If a dedicated 'documentdb' MCP server exists in your environment you would use that profile; otherwise the standard Azure MCP server/profile should be able to run az cosmosdb and inspect the account. (Answer uncertain — environment-specific.)

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's JSON document database service; it was rebranded/expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. 'DocumentDB' as an OSS project is distinct from Azure's hosted service. Today 'DocumentDB' is commonly used interchangeably with Cosmos DB's SQL API legacy name, but Azure Cosmos DB is the umbrella managed service which includes the MongoDB-compatible API.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the hood Cosmos DB uses Microsoft’s proprietary distributed storage and engine with a protocol translation layer for MongoDB compatibility. This means application code using standard MongoDB drivers generally works for supported commands, but some server behavior, performance characteristics, and unsupported MongoDB features may require code changes or workarounds (e.g. limited transactions, aggregation differences, indexing nuances).

answers.question: Which client driver and exact connection-reading code will the sample use to connect to the cluster at runtime?
answers.answer: Use the Python pymongo driver. Read the MongoDB URI from the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable and pass it directly into pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). Example code: from pymongo import MongoClient; import os; client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). Use the sample database 'sample_banking_08'.

answers.question: What database and collection names will the sample create/use?
answers.answer: Database: sample_banking_08. Collections: positions (holds fixed/floating positions and their maturity), scenarios (scenario definitions), reports (generated structured scenario analysis outputs).

answers.question: What index definitions will the sample ensure exist for efficient aggregation?
answers.answer: Create typical single-field indexes used by the aggregation queries: positions.create_index([('maturity_date', 1)]); positions.create_index([('position_type', 1)]); positions.create_index([('currency', 1)]) to support grouping and filtering by maturity bucket, type and currency. (No native vector index assumed.)

answers.question: How will the sample implement vector similarity if needed for embeddings?
answers.answer: Because native vector indexes are not assumed supported, embeddings (if used) will be stored as dense numeric arrays in a field (e.g. embedding) and nearest-neighbour search will be implemented by pulling candidate documents and computing similarity client-side, or by calling an external vector search service (e.g. Azure Cognitive Search custom vector pipeline or a separate vector DB).

answers.question: What Python libraries and exact pip install command will the sample require?
answers.answer: Install pymongo and langchain (and openai or other LLM client) in the venv. Example: pip install pymongo langchain openai python-dotenv. If using azure identity/management or az cli interaction: pip install azure-identity azure-mgmt-cosmosdb.
